chapter_theme: Dread of evil deeds (தீவினையச்சம்): harm done to creatures returns in kind, and bad company is itself a source of evil, turning even the upright. The chapter ends by urging the heart to give up household attachment, since only good done profits the soul.
structure_note: Three quatrains give retribution in kind for harming creatures: eating flesh (121), caging birds (122), eating crabs (123). Five more (124 to 129) concern company and friendship; Mudaliar on 125 says the chapter's point there is to fear the friendship of the small. 130 closes with an address to the heart.

121.reading: The burning grounds are full of the corpses of people who linger in sorrow and do not turn to renunciation, and the bellies of senseless, petty-minded people are burning grounds for the beasts and birds they eat.

positions.position: The sorrow in which people linger is household life itself; Mudaliar also says the verse rejects meat-eating.
The sorrow is the world's suffering in general, in which people are bewildered.

121.nuance: The two halves mirror each other: people end in the burning ground, and the eater's belly becomes a burning ground for animals. The image says that the meat-eater carries a cremation ground inside.

122.reading: Those who catch partridges and quails that live in the humming forest and keep them in cages will go, with irons clanking on their legs, as slaves to strangers into the fields.
122.nuance: The punishment mirrors the crime: those who confined free birds are themselves confined and made to serve. Mudaliar reads கரும்பு ஆர் கழனி as sugarcane fields, and as an alternative as barren and fertile lands; Pope follows the barren reading. Shanmuganar places the punishment in the next birth; the verse doesn't say when.

123.reading: When the old deed of loving to eat crabs and breaking their legs comes home, people get the painful skin disease, white like conch beads, their fingers rotting away and only the palms left.
123.nuance: Again the punishment copies the act: the crab's legs were broken, and the eater's fingers rot. Mudaliar and Shanmuganar read அக்கே போல் as like conch beads; Pope has palms that glow like fire.

124.reading: Even ghee, when it meets fire, burns and causes painful wounds; so even upright people turn and do widely cruel deeds when they join those of harsh deeds.
124.nuance: Mudaliar notes the force of the image: ghee is what soothes burns, so the very thing that heals becomes what wounds. The verse makes company stronger than character.

125.reading: The friendship of the great grows day by day in due order like the crescent moon, while the bond with the small wanes by itself day by day like the full moon moving across the sky.
125.nuance: The word தானே says the waning needs no cause: such a bond decays of itself.

126.reading: You attached yourself to someone, thinking him one of the worthy; if the worth is not in him, listen, it is like opening a casket expecting sandal paste and finding a snake inside.
126.nuance: The repeated சார்ந்தாய் ('you who attached yourself') is a reproach: the fault lies partly with the one who did not examine before attaching.

127.reading: Who is there with the power to examine another's mind and know it? Listen, lord of the land where heavy gems glitter on the slopes: people's minds are one thing and their deeds another.
127.nuance: The gap between mind and deed is offered as the reason minds cannot be known: behaviour is no evidence.

128.reading: The lavish friendship of those who do not join you at heart but act with an eye to their own gain, befriending you with guile, turns into a stain on the mind, lord of the flowering hills.
128.nuance: Whose mind is stained is left open. Mudaliar says the friendship itself becomes a fault, Shanmuganar that it grows tainted and perishes, and Pope that it brings disappointment to those deceived.

129.reading: If a raised, gleaming sword falls into an enemy's hand it truly destroys one's strength; since ஆக்கம் among the unlearned burns one in both worlds, the good course is to get away from them.

positions.position: ஆக்கம் means joining the unlearned, and that association is what burns.
ஆக்கம் is one's own growth, which friendship with the unlearned burns up in both worlds.

129.nuance: Pope offers a third sense, wealth bestowed on the foolish. On every reading the sword image says that what should protect you turns against you once it is in the wrong hands.

130.reading: Heart, you won't let go of attachment to home, and you pine for the sake of children; for how many ages do you think you'll live? Apart from the good one has done, however small, there is no real gain for a living being.
130.nuance: Both commentators read மனைப்பாசம் as attachment to one's wife. The verse doesn't call family evil; it says family is not the gain the soul carries.

links.note: On Mudaliar's reading, 121 makes household life itself the sorrow in which those who fail to renounce end as corpses. 46 asks what anyone would gain by leaving a household life lived in virtue for the other path. The tension depends on Mudaliar's gloss of துக்கம்; on Shanmuganar's it is weaker.
Both condemn eating flesh. The Kural asks how one who fattens his flesh on others' can have grace; the Naladiyar makes his belly a burning ground.
Both say harm done to others returns to the doer. The Naladiyar makes the return copy the harm: those who caged birds wear irons.
Both explain a wretched diseased body as the result of having taken life. The Naladiyar names the creature and the disease.
Both say a person takes on the nature of their company, the Kural with water changing with the soil and the Naladiyar with ghee turning to flame.

112 says the worthy never fall from their nature, as jaggery is never bitter. 124 says even the upright turn to cruel deeds when they join the wicked. Both concern whether good character can be changed; the tension holds if 124's கோடார் are truly good, as Mudaliar's நடுவுநிலைமையுடையார் implies.
124 shows company corrupting the upright; 139 shows it improving the unlearned, like a new pot taking on the scent of flowers. The same mechanism works in both directions.
Both use the waxing and waning moon for good and bad friendship. The Kural sets the wise against fools, and the Naladiyar the great against the small.
Both warn of friendship formed without examination; the Kural says it ends in mortal grief, the Naladiyar finds a snake where sandal was expected.

127 says no one can know another's mind, because minds and deeds differ. 706 says the face shows what is uppermost in the heart, as crystal shows what is near it. The tension depends on taking 127 as a general claim rather than a warning about deceivers.
702 grants that someone may know another's mind without doubt, but calls such a person equal to a god. 127 says no one has that power, which agrees that it is beyond ordinary people.
Both describe friendship without inner consent. The Kural calls it an anvil waiting for the right moment to strike; the Naladiyar says it becomes a stain.
Both use a bright sword in the wrong hands. In the Kural it is learning held by one who fears the assembly; in the Naladiyar it is one's own strength lost through association with the unlearned.
Both prefer distance from fools to closeness: the Kural rates the enmity of the wise far above a fool's intimacy, and the Naladiyar says the good course is to get away from the unlearned.

61 says no gain is known greater than children who learn what should be known. 130 rebukes the heart for pining for children and says there is no gain for the soul but good done. The tension softens if 61 speaks of worldly gains and 130 only of the soul's.

source_issues: 129: Mudaliar's commentary breaks off mid-word at நற்செய.
Shanmuganar's verse numbers in this chapter run 51 to 60, and 130's Shanmuganar field ends with the heading of the next chapter.
